n: The creation is complete. The “host” means everything that fills the heavens and earth—stars, creatures, and all. The chapter division here interrupts the creation story, which really ends at verse 3.

f.g: A great company or army; here, all the things that fill heaven and earth.

n: God “rests” on the seventh day—not because He is tired, but because the work is finished. His rest sets a pattern for His children to stop their labors and turn to Him.

f.g: Hebrew shavat — to stop or cease; the root of “Sabbath.”

n: God blesses the seventh day and makes it holy. This is the root of the Sabbath, a weekly reminder that time itself belongs to God and that creation is His gift.

f.g: Made holy; set apart for a sacred purpose.

n: A new section begins, using a new name for God: “the LORD God.” In KJV small capitals, LORD stands for the sacred name Jehovah, whom Latter-day Saints understand to be the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.g: Hebrew toledot — “account” or “family history.” This phrase marks new sections throughout Genesis (5:1; 6:9; 10:1; 11:10).
Hebrew YHWH Elohim. Printed LORD in capitals to signal the divine name.

n: Plants did not yet grow in the fields, since there was no rain and no one to farm. The book of Moses explains that God first created all things spiritually before they existed naturally on the earth.

f.w: before it was in the earth

f.g: To plow and work the soil.

n: Water rises from the ground to moisten the land, preparing it for life even before rain.

f.g: Hebrew ’ed — perhaps a spring or stream rising from the ground; the meaning is uncertain.

n: God shapes the man from earth like a potter and breathes life into him. Body and spirit together make a “living soul,” an idea restoration scripture makes explicit: the spirit and body are the soul of man.

f.g: Hebrew yatsar — to shape, as a potter shapes clay.
Wordplay: ’adam (man) is formed from ’adamah (ground).

n: God plants a garden in Eden, toward the east, and places the man there. The garden is a place of God’s presence—like a first temple.

f.g: The name likely means “delight” or “pleasure.”

n: The garden is beautiful and full of food. In its center stand two special trees: the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil. These two trees will set up the choice that follows.

f.w: the tree of knowledge of good and evil

n: A single river flows out of Eden and divides into four. Water flowing from God’s presence becomes a recurring image of life-giving blessing.

f.w: a river went out of Eden

f.g: Headwaters or branches of a river.

n: The first river, Pison, winds around the land of Havilah, known for its gold. Its location is uncertain today.

f.g: Goes around; winds through.
A region probably in or near Arabia (compare Genesis 10:7, 29).

n: Havilah’s riches are listed: fine gold, a fragrant resin, and precious stones. Such materials later adorn the tabernacle and the high priest’s clothing.

f.g: Probably a fragrant, pale resin (compare Numbers 11:7).

n: The second river, Gihon, flows around “Ethiopia,” here translating Cush. The exact region intended is debated.

f.g: Hebrew Cush, which can mean Ethiopia/Nubia or a region in Mesopotamia.

n: The third river, Hiddekel, is the Tigris, and the fourth is the Euphrates—both well-known rivers of Mesopotamia. These names root the story in a real geography.

f.g: The Tigris River (compare Daniel 10:4).

n: Adam is given work in paradise: to tend and protect the garden. Meaningful labor is part of God’s design for humanity, not just a result of the Fall.

f.w: to dress it and to keep it
f.g: To work and to guard it. The same Hebrew verbs later describe priests serving and guarding the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8).

n: God speaks to Adam with great generosity first: every tree is available. The commandment that follows comes within a setting of abundance.

f.g: Without restriction.

n: Only one tree is forbidden, and eating it will bring death. The book of Moses adds that God told Adam he could still choose for himself—agency is part of the plan.

f.g: Abraham 5:13 notes this was reckoned by the Lord’s time, in which a day may be a thousand years.

n: For the first time something is “not good”: being alone. God plans a partner who corresponds to the man and stands beside him as an equal help.

f.g: “Meet” = suitable or fitting. Hebrew ʿezer kenegdo — a helper corresponding to him, “face to face.” ʿEzer is also used of God helping Israel.

n: God brings the animals to Adam to name them. Naming shows Adam’s God-given stewardship and also prepares him to notice what is missing.

f.w: to see what he would call them
f.g: God gives Adam real responsibility and respects his choices.

n: Adam names every animal, but none is a true partner for him. The search highlights how unique the woman will be.

f.g: Here becomes a personal name; Hebrew ’adam also means “man” or “mankind.”

n: God puts Adam into a deep sleep and takes part of his side. Adam does not witness the woman’s creation; she is entirely God’s work.

f.g: Hebrew tselaʿ — side. The image suggests the woman stands at the man’s side, neither above nor below him. President Spencer W. Kimball taught that the rib account is figurative.

n: God fashions the woman and brings her to the man, as a father might present a bride. This is the first marriage, performed by God Himself.
Adam bursts into the Bible’s first poetry with joy: at last, someone like him! The Hebrew wordplay ’ishah (woman) and ’ish (man) shows their deep kinship.

f.w: bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh
f.g: A Hebrew idiom for close family relationship (compare 2 Samuel 5:1).
Hebrew ’ishah, from ’ish, “man.”

n: The narrator draws a lasting lesson: marriage creates a new, primary bond. Jesus quoted this verse to teach that God joins husband and wife.

f.g: A complete union of life—physical, emotional, and spiritual.

n: In their innocence the man and woman feel no shame. This sets up the change that comes in the next chapter after the Fall.

f.g: Hebrew ʿarumim — a wordplay with the “subtil” (ʿarum) serpent in 3:1.
